{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"# Choice screens are not market choice

A choice screen is a menu, not a market. The distinction matters because menus have editors, defaults, and missing items. A company can offer you five browsers, six app stores, or twelve payment systems while retaining the power that counts: deciding which choices become visible, credible, and easy. If it owns the frame, it still owns much of the game.

Start with selection. Who chooses the listed options? Usually, the gatekeeper sets eligibility rules, technical interfaces, ranking criteria, and deadlines (all of which can look neutral in isolation). A rival may appear only after accepting the gatekeeper’s contract, fees, telemetry, and design constraints. You get to pick, but only from the candidates admitted to somebody else’s ballot – a ballot whose printer can reject inconvenient names. That isn’t open competition. It’s curated competition, and the curator remains sovereign.

Defaults do the rest. Developers know this in their bones: the preselected path gets traffic, and every warning, permission prompt, or extra click sheds users. Suppose your phone shows a choice screen during setup. If the incumbent is first, already signed in, and described as “recommended,” while the alternative requires another account (plus a scary consent dialog), your nominal freedom has been loaded like a pair of dice. You can still roll them. You just can’t expect a fair game.

This is why measuring choice by counting logos is bullshit. Ten options can conceal one decision-maker; two options can represent real rivalry if neither party controls access to the customer. I think the useful question is simpler: which power changes hands. If you can select a service but can’t remove the gatekeeper’s surveillance, payment rail, or veto, you haven’t escaped the gate. You have decorated it, possibly with a jaunty new icon.

Think of a landlord who offers tenants a “choice” of locksmiths. The list sounds generous. But the landlord chooses who qualifies, requires every locksmith to use the landlord’s master key, and reserves the right to revoke any key remotely. Your choice might affect the color of the handle or the speed of service. It doesn’t alter who can enter the building. A platform choice screen can work the same way – consumer preference at the surface, gatekeeper control underneath.

To be fair, a well-designed screen can help. It can tell you alternatives exist, interrupt automatic enrollment, and give a smaller supplier a moment of attention. I wouldn’t throw that away. But disclosure is a remedy for ignorance, not domination. When the underlying firm still writes the admission rules, owns the customer relationship, and can punish successful rivals, the screen treats the visible symptom while preserving the machinery that produced it.

A meaningful remedy changes capabilities, not cosmetics. It lets users install software and switch defaults after setup; lets competing services reach customers without discriminatory tolls; lets people move their data in usable formats; and prevents a gatekeeper from grading its own products on a curve. The exact rules will vary by system (a package manager isn’t a payment network), but the test should stay concrete: can a rival serve you without asking its competitor for continuing permission?

That also means enforcement can’t stop at launch day. A gatekeeper can comply with the visible screen and then make the chosen option slower, less integrated, or harder to update (death by a thousand API papercuts). We need rules against retaliation, auditable criteria for access, and consequences large enough that exclusion won’t remain the profitable option. Otherwise, we’re asking the casino to post fair odds while letting it weight the roulette wheel – and inspect its own workshop.

I use one final test: after the remedy, who must ask whom? If every competitor still needs the dominant platform’s blessing, if your preferred tool still runs at its sufferance, or if our exit still leaves our data and purchases behind, then we haven’t created market choice. We’ve created a nicer supplication form. I’d keep the screen, certainly, but I’d stop pretending the screen is the reform. That is the difference between being offered buttons and holding rights: buttons can be rearranged overnight, while rights constrain the party that originally designed the entire interface. # Choice screens are not market choice

A choice screen is a menu, not a market. The distinction matters because menus have editors, defaults, and missing items. A company can offer you five browsers, six app stores, or twelve payment systems while retaining the power that counts: deciding which choices become visible, credible, and easy. If it owns the frame, it still owns much of the game.

Start with selection. Who chooses the listed options? Usually, the gatekeeper sets eligibility rules, technical interfaces, ranking criteria, and deadlines (all of which can look neutral in isolation). A rival may appear only after accepting the gatekeeper’s contract, fees, telemetry, and design constraints. You get to pick, but only from the candidates admitted to somebody else’s ballot – a ballot whose printer can reject inconvenient names. That isn’t open competition. It’s curated competition, and the curator remains sovereign.

Defaults do the rest. Developers know this in their bones: the preselected path gets traffic, and every warning, permission prompt, or extra click sheds users. Suppose your phone shows a choice screen during setup. If the incumbent is first, already signed in, and described as “recommended,” while the alternative requires another account (plus a scary consent dialog), your nominal freedom has been loaded like a pair of dice. You can still roll them. You just can’t expect a fair game.

This is why measuring choice by counting logos is bullshit. Ten options can conceal one decision-maker; two options can represent real rivalry if neither party controls access to the customer. I think the useful question is simpler: which power changes hands. If you can select a service but can’t remove the gatekeeper’s surveillance, payment rail, or veto, you haven’t escaped the gate. You have decorated it, possibly with a jaunty new icon.

Think of a landlord who offers tenants a “choice” of locksmiths. The list sounds generous. But the landlord chooses who qualifies, requires every locksmith to use the landlord’s master key, and reserves the right to revoke any key remotely. Your choice might affect the color of the handle or the speed of service. It doesn’t alter who can enter the building. A platform choice screen can work the same way – consumer preference at the surface, gatekeeper control underneath.

To be fair, a well-designed screen can help. It can tell you alternatives exist, interrupt automatic enrollment, and give a smaller supplier a moment of attention. I wouldn’t throw that away. But disclosure is a remedy for ignorance, not domination. When the underlying firm still writes the admission rules, owns the customer relationship, and can punish successful rivals, the screen treats the visible symptom while preserving the machinery that produced it.

A meaningful remedy changes capabilities, not cosmetics. It lets users install software and switch defaults after setup; lets competing services reach customers without discriminatory tolls; lets people move their data in usable formats; and prevents a gatekeeper from grading its own products on a curve. The exact rules will vary by system (a package manager isn’t a payment network), but the test should stay concrete: can a rival serve you without asking its competitor for continuing permission?

That also means enforcement can’t stop at launch day. A gatekeeper can comply with the visible screen and then make the chosen option slower, less integrated, or harder to update (death by a thousand API papercuts). We need rules against retaliation, auditable criteria for access, and consequences large enough that exclusion won’t remain the profitable option. Otherwise, we’re asking the casino to post fair odds while letting it weight the roulette wheel – and inspect its own workshop.

I use one final test: after the remedy, who must ask whom? If every competitor still needs the dominant platform’s blessing, if your preferred tool still runs at its sufferance, or if our exit still leaves our data and purchases behind, then we haven’t created market choice. We’ve created a nicer supplication form. I’d keep the screen, certainly, but I’d stop pretending the screen is the reform. That is the difference between being offered buttons and holding rights: buttons can be rearranged overnight, while rights constrain the party that originally designed the entire interface. Choice is meaningful only when choosing changes who has power.
